day-25-act-01.title: Sample spaces, events, and counting
day-25-act-01.prerequisites: Complete Day 24 (linear algebra wrap-up); if blocked, review Day 21 before continuing.
day-25-act-01.objective: Define a sample space, enumerate equally likely outcomes, and compute event probabilities by counting under explicitly stated fairness and independence assumptions.
day-25-act-01.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-25-act-01.instructions: Study source: within this activity's existing reading/practice time, use Stat 110: Strategic Practice and Homework Problems, Strategic Practice and Homework 1; linked problem and solution document, then explain one connection to the local task in your own words. Keep the local exercise and acceptance checks; use its original explanation if the external source is unavailable. A probability model assumes a sample space $\Omega$ of equally likely outcomes and assigns $P(A) = |A|/|\Omega|$ to an event $A$. For two fair and independent six-sided dice, the sample space is the 36 ordered pairs $(a,b)$, each with probability $1/36$; fair marginals alone are insufficient: if the dice always match, the sum-7 probability is 0 and the at-least-one-6 probability is $1/6$. Required work: predict the counts first, then enumerate the pairs whose sum is 7 and the pairs containing at least one 6 (use inclusion-exclusion so $(6,6)$ is not double-counted). Optional work: repeat the counting exercise with three coins only after the required evidence is complete.
day-25-act-01.exercise_prompt: For two fair and independent six-sided dice (so each ordered pair has probability $1/36$), predict then compute: (a) $P(\text{sum}=7)$; (b) $P(\text{at least one die shows }6)$. Give each answer as a fraction of the 36 ordered pairs and as a decimal, and state the fairness and independence assumptions you relied on.
day-25-act-01.hint: Sum-7 ordered pairs are (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1). For at least one 6: 6 pairs have first die 6, 6 have second die 6, minus the double-counted (6,6).
day-25-act-01.answer: (a) $P(\text{sum}=7) = 6/36 = 1/6 \approx 0.1667$. (b) $P(\text{at least one }6) = 11/36 \approx 0.3056$ (inclusion-exclusion: $6+6-1=11$). Both verified by enumerating all 36 ordered pairs under the stated fair-and-independent-dice assumption.
day-25-act-01.mastery_criterion: Your sample space is the 36 ordered pairs; both probabilities are derived by counting under the explicitly stated assumptions that each die is fair and the dice are independent (equivalently, each pair has probability 1/36), not recalled.

day-25-act-02.title: Conditional probability and independence
day-25-act-02.prerequisites: Complete the previous activity; if blocked, follow Activity 01’s Day 21 review guidance before continuing.
day-25-act-02.objective: Compute $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$ by restricting the sample space, and verify independence through the product identity $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
day-25-act-02.instructions: Study source: within this activity's existing reading/practice time, use Stat 110: Strategic Practice and Homework Problems, Strategic Practice and Homework 2: Conditional Probability; problems and solutions, then explain one connection to the local task in your own words. Keep the local exercise and acceptance checks; use its original explanation if the external source is unavailable. Conditioning on $B$ shrinks the sample space to $B$ and renormalizes: work inside the reduced space rather than memorizing formulas. Required work: solve (a)-(c) below unaided, writing for each which restricted sample space you used. Independence is a numerical identity to verify, not an intuition to assert.
day-25-act-02.exercise_prompt: Two fair and independent dice (so each ordered pair has probability 1/36). (a) Given the first die is even, find $P(\text{sum}=8)$. (b) Given the sum is 7, find $P(\text{first die}=4)$. (c) Are 'first die even' and 'sum=7' independent? Compare $P(\text{even})\cdot P(\text{sum}=7)$ with $P(\text{even}\cap\text{sum}=7)$.
day-25-act-02.hint: (a) First-die-even leaves 18 pairs; sum-8 among them: (2,6),(4,4),(6,2). (c) Sum-7 with even first die: (2,5),(4,3),(6,1) - count 3.
day-25-act-02.answer: (a) $3/18 = 1/6 \approx 0.1667$. (b) $1/6 \approx 0.1667$. (c) $P(\text{even})\cdot P(\text{sum}=7) = (1/2)(1/6) = 1/12$ equals $P(\text{even}\cap\text{sum}=7) = 3/36 = 1/12$, so the events are independent - verified by the product identity, not assumed.
day-25-act-02.mastery_criterion: All three results are derived unaided by restricted counting; independence is claimed only after the product check $1/12 = 3/36$, with the conditioning set named for each part.

day-25-act-03.title: Bayes' rule and empirical frequency vs. probability
day-25-act-03.prerequisites: Complete the previous activity; if blocked, follow Activity 01’s Day 21 review guidance before continuing.
day-25-act-03.objective: Apply Bayes' rule $P(D\mid +)=P(+\mid D)P(D)/P(+)$ with a total-probability denominator, then run a seeded simulation to separate empirical frequencies from guaranteed probabilities.
day-25-act-03.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-25-act-03.instructions: Screening example: prevalence $P(D)=0.01$, sensitivity $P(+\mid D)=0.99$, false-positive rate $P(+\mid \bar D)=0.05$. Compute $P(+)$ by total probability, then $P(D\mid +)$. Then run: python3 -c "import random; random.seed(25); pairs=[(random.randint(1,6), random.randint(1,6)) for _ in range(36)]; print(sum(1 for a,b in pairs if a+b==7))" and compare the observed frequency of sum-7 with $1/6$.
day-25-act-03.exercise_prompt: (a) Compute $P(D\mid +)$ for the screening scenario. (b) Report the seeded frequency of sum-7 in 36 simulated pairs and explain why it need not equal $1/6$. (c) If an event is never observed in $n$ trials, is its probability exactly zero?
day-25-act-03.hint: $P(+) = 0.99\cdot0.01 + 0.05\cdot0.99 = 0.0594$. For (c): an unobserved event is not a guaranteed zero-probability event - this is the zero-count problem.
day-25-act-03.answer: (a) $P(D\mid +) = 0.0099/0.0594 = 1/6 \approx 0.1667$: at 1% prevalence most positive results are false alarms. (b) With seed 25, 8 of 36 pairs sum to 7: frequency $0.2222 \neq 1/6 \approx 0.1667$ - frequencies fluctuate around probabilities rather than matching them. (c) No: zero observed successes do not bound the unknown probability deterministically; a rare event can go unobserved in n trials. Any bound needs a stated model and confidence level: under the model of n i.i.d. Bernoulli trials with the same unknown p, for positive integer n, K~Binomial(n,p) and P_p(K=0)=(1-p)^n. After observing K=0, the exact one-sided 95% upper confidence limit is U=1-0.05^(1/n), obtained by solving (1-U)^n=0.05. The rule of three, U≈-ln(0.05)/n≈3/n, is a large-n, small-U approximation, not a deterministic proof; 3/n is not a valid unqualified probability when 3/n>1. Without the stated i.i.d. Bernoulli assumptions, this binomial confidence limit and the 3/n approximation are not justified by this argument; a bound under another model needs its own justification - e.g. 100 perfectly correlated observations (all copies of one shared draw) with true p=0.5 show zero successes with probability 0.5, although 3/n=0.03. Separately, smoothing avoids assigning literal zero.
day-25-act-03.mastery_criterion: Bayes arithmetic shows a total-probability denominator; the observed simulation frequency is reported honestly; the zero-count caveat and the frequency/probability distinction are stated in your own words.

day-25-act-04.title: Independent mastery check: probability foundations
day-25-act-04.prerequisites: Complete the previous activity; if blocked, follow Activity 01’s Day 21 review guidance before continuing.
day-25-act-04.objective: Solve unseen probability problems unaided, stating every assumption (priors, likelihoods, independence) used.
day-25-act-04.instructions: No AI, references, or calculators beyond arithmetic during this check. Solve all three items, record predictions before verifying, then review errors and follow a recovery link for any missed idea. Preserve the first unaided attempt unchanged; afterwards, error review and any assisted recovery are a distinct phase, and a missed idea counts as remediated only after a fresh equivalent unaided check whose answer is not shown in advance. Second check (only after remediation; unaided, no hints): (a) $P(\text{spam})=0.3$, $P(w\mid\text{spam})=0.8$, $P(w\mid\text{ham})=0.2$: compute $P(\text{spam}\mid w)$. (b) Two cards drawn without replacement from a 52-card deck: compute $P(\text{both hearts})$. (c) For a naive Bayes score using two words $w_1,w_2$, write the factorisation it assumes and one reason it fails for real text. This card gives no answer for the second check: grade it by the same standard as the mastery criterion (exact values from the stated model, every assumption written), and verify only after finishing, by a second method (a 1000-message frequency table, or counting ordered pairs). Remediate a missed (a) with day-25-act-03 (Bayes' rule, total-probability denominator), (b) with day-25-act-02 (dependent events) and day-25-act-01 (counting), and (c) with day-25-act-02 (independence).
day-25-act-04.exercise_prompt: (a) A spam filter: $P(\text{spam})=0.2$, $P(w\mid\text{spam})=0.9$ for a suspicious word $w$, $P(w\mid\text{ham})=0.1$. Compute $P(\text{spam}\mid w)$. (b) Two cards drawn without replacement from a 52-card deck: compute $P(\text{both aces})$. (c) For a multi-feature naive Bayes classifier scoring a message with several suspicious words, state the conditional-independence assumption it adds, and say whether it is realistic. ((a) used a single feature, so its posterior comes from Bayes' rule alone.)
day-25-act-04.hint: (a) $P(w) = 0.9\cdot0.2 + 0.1\cdot0.8 = 0.26$. (b) Draws without replacement are dependent: multiply $4/52$ by $3/51$.
day-25-act-04.answer: (a) $P(\text{spam}\mid w) = 0.18/0.26 = 9/13 \approx 0.6923$. (b) $(4/52)(3/51) = 1/221 \approx 0.00452$. (c) In the multi-feature case, naive Bayes assumes feature occurrences are conditionally independent given the class; the single-feature posterior in (a) needed no such assumption - it follows from Bayes' rule alone. The assumption is computationally convenient but only approximately true for real text.
day-25-act-04.mastery_criterion: Unaided answers match $9/13$ and $1/221$; the assumed model (prior, likelihoods, conditional independence, sampling without replacement) is stated explicitly; misses route to a recovery link, and each missed idea is remediated only by a fresh equivalent unaided check.
